content.comment_body: I was told this is likely a memory leak, apparently something known to [company_name]. I'm not sure. Yesterday I switched the hardware to [version_no] and now it's working. The hardware switch took 2 hours, while switching the software from [version_no] to [version_no] took 8 hours—overall, a very challenging process. I'm running Linux on a MacBook, so there's no CD or DVD drive. To update, since the old software was on another machine, you have to find a device with a DVD drive, copy the DVD to a USB flash drive, then install from USB on the new PC. Afterwards, you need to download an update and apply it. Once that's finally complete, it's necessary to read manuals and look up online advice to get the [company_name] software running, as they only support a specific Linux distribution. You have to modify network configurations or make the software believe it's on that supported system (for no clear reason). Also, you need to be on the same network—it's impossible to run [product_name] Web Editor from a different subnet. Even though the programming software can connect and reports everything is fine, it still doesn't work. It felt like a major ordeal just to make the first download after switching to the new hardware. Of course, the older laptop running [version_no] software isn't compatible with the [version_no] hardware. It was a rough day, full of frustration. In the end, the status of the relays is still unknown, and the program itself remains unchanged.

Running Linux on a MacBook and using a program mainly designed for Windows is impressive. Is there a runtime environment that lets you run Windows programs on a Mac, or have you tried using a virtual machine? That could help avoid many of these issues. Regards, [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: The user faced major challenges updating [product_name] software and hardware to newer versions on an unsupported operating system. The process was complicated, especially since Linux on a MacBook isn't among officially supported platforms. Issues included incompatibilities between software and hardware versions, tedious steps for installation and licensing due to legacy media formats, and limited network configuration options, all combining to create a poor user experience.
analysis.user_expectations: The user desires a simpler, more compatible, and flexible upgrade and installation process for [product_name] software, with better support for modern operating systems and easier network configuration.
pain_keywords: lack of support for modern OS
